title: Simulation or postselection universality for algebraic two-qubit interactions
formal: For every fixed Hermitian \(4\times4\) matrix \(H\) with complex algebraic entries, does at least one of the following hold: all of its basis-input, basis-output circuits admit polynomial-time classical sampling to arbitrary inverse-polynomial total-variation accuracy; or \(\mathrm{PP}\subseteq\operatorname{Post}(H)\), with the circuit, uniformity and postselection conventions below?
why: Seeks a boundary between classically manageable quantum dynamics and postselection universality using only one fixed two-qubit interaction. The restriction to basis preparation and measurement makes computational power depend on more than ordinary unitary controllability.
status_note: A user-authorized precise variant of the 2016/2017 general interaction question. The primary commuting theorem and the later analog theorem have different scopes and do not establish this selected general dichotomy. Reviewed on 13 September 2026; the model choices are editorial and no exhaustive current-status claim is made.

importance.reason: A broad classification question for the computational power of restricted quantum interactions; an exact simulation convention is needed for a benchmark-ready dichotomy. Existing score retained.

sentences: A fixed two-qubit interaction generates circuits by evolving selected ordered pairs for specified times.
Every circuit begins in a computational-basis state and ends with computational-basis measurement.
The chosen dichotomy asks for efficient classical approximate sampling or full PP decision power with postselection.
The variant makes all matrix constants, time encodings, sampling accuracy and conditioning probabilities explicit.
Commuting-interaction results and analog Hamiltonian simulations do not by themselves classify this unrestricted circuit model.

definitions: The matrix \(H=H^*\) is fixed, not part of a circuit input. Its entries are algebraic complex numbers, specified by finite integer-polynomial and isolating-region descriptions that may be hardcoded into an algorithm depending on \(H\). A circuit has \(N\ge1\) qubits initialized to an explicitly supplied computational-basis string \(b\in\{0,1\}^N\). Each gate chooses an ordered pair of distinct qubits and applies \(\exp(-itH)\) on that pair for a signed rational time \(t\); negative times give exact inverse evolution. There are no free single-qubit gates or intermediate measurements. At the end all qubits are measured in the computational basis, defining a probability distribution \(p_C\) on \(\{0,1\}^N\). The input explicitly lists the initial bits, gate sequence, ordered wire indices and rational numerators and positive denominators in binary. It also includes a unary integer \(B\ge1\) with \(|t|\le B\) for every gate. Let \(L\) be the full bit encoding length. This charges enough description length for polynomial physical evolution time, as required by the source model. The simulation branch requires a single uniform randomized Turing machine for this fixed \(H\), taking \(C\) and a binary rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), that halts on every random tape within a fixed polynomial in \(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\) and outputs a string with distribution \(s_C\) satisfying \(\tfrac12\sum_z|s_C(z)-p_C(z)|\le\varepsilon\). It uses independent fair coins and no oracle or advice. Define \(\operatorname{Post}(H)\) as follows. For a language \(K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a uniform deterministic polynomial-time compiler maps each input \(x\) to such a circuit \(C_x\), a designated output bit, and a disjoint list of postselection bits with prescribed values. There is a polynomial \(p\) such that the prescribed event has probability at least \(2^{-p(|x|)}\) on every input. Conditional on it, the output is 1 with probability at least \(2/3\) for \(x\in K\) and at most \(1/3\) otherwise. Circuit descriptions, including the unary time bound, have polynomial length in \(|x|\). The postselection list and values may depend on the input through the compiler. PP consists of languages for which a uniform polynomial-time fair-coin Turing machine accepts with probability strictly greater than \(1/2\) on members and at most \(1/2\) on nonmembers. The second branch is the source’s postselected-computation criterion expressed via PP; the algebraic-entry, accuracy and exponentially bounded postselection conventions are explicit editorial choices. The alternatives need not be disjoint. No commutativity promise is imposed on \(H\).
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the disjunction for every allowed fixed interaction, or a Lean counterexample interaction for which both branches fail. The proof must use the supplied finite-precision sampling and uniform postselection conventions. A classification with free local gates, arbitrary analog reductions, a commutativity promise or a different sampling error does not automatically settle this variant.

context_blocks.text: The original question asks whether every fixed two-qubit interaction is classically simulable or universal with postselection. Its circuit model starts and ends in the computational basis and permits oriented interactions and inverse evolution.

The authorized editorial variant fixes algebraic matrix entries, rational gate times with a charged physical-time bound, total-variation sampling accuracy and an exponential lower bound on the conditioning event. These choices specify a discrete benchmark; they are not asserted to be the source’s only interpretation.
The later analog-universality theorem classifies a different simulation model with closed Hamiltonian families and faithful reductions.
